notes.title: Op-Ed: On the Geopolitical Trajectory
body: The latest US strikes represent a predictable enforcement of red lines on Hormuz freedom of navigation, but they also highlight the fragility of the June MoU—deals built on temporary waivers and 60-day windows are vulnerable to spoilers and asymmetric tactics.

US strategy has shown leverage through military and economic pressure (blockade, strikes, sanctions tools), yet repeated cycles risk mission creep and higher long-term costs; a durable settlement likely requires addressing core Iranian concerns (nuclear pathway, sanctions relief, regional influence) alongside US and Israeli security demands.

Economically, the conflict has been a textbook stagflationary impulse—higher energy prices weigh on growth while boosting inflation, with Europe bearing a heavier burden due to import reliance. Quick de-escalation is the best antidote to entrenched expectations.

For central banks: The Fed and ECB should “look through” transitory energy spikes where possible but monitor second-round risks closely; premature easing could complicate credibility if volatility persists.

Broader lesson: Chokepoint vulnerabilities (Hormuz) amplify global spillovers in a multipolar world. Diversification of energy routes/supply and stronger multilateral crisis mechanisms would reduce future tail risks.

Path forward: Pragmatic incrementalism (extended talks, confidence measures on shipping/sanctions) beats maximalist goals. Both sides have incentives to stabilize—US to avoid broader entanglement ahead of domestic timelines, Iran to ease economic isolation. The alternative is costly attrition that benefits no one long-term.
Markets and policymakers should price in persistent uncertainty rather than assuming linear progress; hedging energy exposure and watching diplomatic signals will be essential in the weeks ahead.
